findings.message: wikilink: [[tttrlib-editable-rebuild]]
findings.source: * **Pixel-wise FLIM MLE: C++ batch fit + threaded dispatch makes fitting scale (in-process, ~4×).** Superseded the earlier fork-multiprocessing approach after finding the real bottleneck. Per-fit threading did not scale (flat 1.0× on 2–8 threads) even with the GIL released around `DecayFit23::fit`: each fit releases the GIL for <1 ms, and the **per-fit GIL-handoff convoy** serialises the threads. Ruled out the macOS nano allocator (`MallocNanoZone=0` unchanged) and `thread_local`/TLS (plain `static` unchanged); a BLAS `np.dot` control thread-scales 4× in the same process, so it was the fit, not the environment. Fix: a new tttrlib batch entry point **`DecayFit23::fit_matrix`** (committed in tttrlib `1650cf67`) fits a whole `(n_rows × 2·n_ch)` matrix in one C++ call with the GIL released for the *entire* loop; rebuild the arm64 editable install per [[tttrlib-editable-rebuild]] (note the SWIG-regen gotcha recorded there — `touch ext/python/tttrlib.i` after editing an included `.i`). ChiSurf side: `Fit2x.fit_many` wraps it, and `chisurf/core/fluorescence/mle/parallel.py::fit_matrix_threaded` splits rows across a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (each thread its own `Fit2x`) — **no multiprocessing**, so no fork/spawn fragility and safe inside the Qt GUI. `img_pixel_mle/core/pixel_mle.py` now dispatches through it (`n_workers` control, `_MIN_ROWS_FOR_THREADS` gate). Measured: batch threading 2t 1.95× / 4t 3.74× / 8t 4.63×, bit-identical to single-fit; end-to-end A/B on `beads.ptu` baseline→+fast 1.15×→+threaded(7w) **4.08×**, results identical. Tests updated (`test_threaded_matches_serial`); benchmark `test/benchmarks/benchmark_pixel_mle.py`. Replaces the fork-MP `fit_matrix_parallel`. See [plugins/imaging.md](/plugins/imaging.md) and the `fit2x` harness in [subsystems/fitting.md](/subsystems/fitting.md).
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: wikilink: [[tttrlib-editable-rebuild]]
findings.source: * **Pixel-wise FLIM MLE throughput: vectorised extraction + multiprocessing fits + GIL release (A/B benchmarked).** Two optimisations to `img_pixel_mle/core/pixel_mle.py`, both A/B-verified to give **identical** per-pixel lifetimes. (1) **Vectorised extraction** — replaced the per-pixel Python `tttr_indices`+`np.bincount` loop with one `CLSMImage.get_fluorescence_decay` C++ call building the whole per-pixel histogram stack (matches bincount exactly; the returned uint8 is guarded — saturation auto-falls-back to the exact bincount engine). An `engine` switch (`"auto"`/`"fast"`/`"loop"`) selects it. (2) **Multiprocessing fits** — the per-pixel `Fit23` calls (the dominant cost) now run across worker processes over a shared-memory copy of the histogram matrix, via a new reusable, Qt-free helper `chisurf/core/fluorescence/mle/parallel.py::fit_matrix_parallel` (built on the `fit2x` harness). It uses the **fork** start method so workers inherit the parent's imports — avoiding a hang where `spawn` re-imports the deep plugin/GUI package chain in a subprocess — with a serial fallback on any failure and an `n_workers` control. **Investigation & tttrlib change:** per the "let it release GIL" steer, added GIL release around `DecayFit{23,24,25,26}::fit` in tttrlib (`ext/python/DecayFit*.i`, committed there `bebd7bb9`; rebuild the arm64 editable install per [[tttrlib-editable-rebuild]]). Threaded fits are now **bit-identical** to serial (the fit's per-call state is `static thread_local`), but in-process threading still does **not scale** on macOS (the fit serialises on an internal per-thread-state access path; a BLAS `np.dot` control thread-scales 4× in the same env, so it is the fit, not the environment) — hence multiprocessing for throughput. The GIL release is kept as the correct, safe precondition (helps latency/GUI-responsiveness; enables future threading if the C++ serialiser is removed). **A/B benchmark** `test/benchmarks/benchmark_pixel_mle.py` on real FLIM `tttr-data/imaging/pq/Microtime200_HH400/beads.ptu`: baseline (loop, serial) → +fast extraction 1.13× → +parallel (7 workers) **2.58×**, results identical. Tests: `img_pixel_mle/test/test_pixel_mle_core.py` gains fast-vs-loop and MP-vs-serial equivalence (6 pass); benchmark has a `slow` equivalence+speedup test. See [plugins/imaging.md](/plugins/imaging.md) and the `fit2x` harness in [subsystems/fitting.md](/subsystems/fitting.md).

findings.message: wikilink: [[viewjson-custom-sections-bind-by-target]]
findings.source: - **Finding:** the reason given for skipping `custom` sections — their "widgets own their own values" — is false for `path_list`, the unified file/folder list: its value is a plain `list[str]` **on the model**, addressed by `target` (see [[viewjson-custom-sections-bind-by-target]]), and is exactly as JSON-safe as any `ValueSection`. Because `_key` keys off `attr`, it is dropped. **12 shipped specs** declare a `path_list`, **10 of them alongside other bound controls**, so they are counted among the 83 "restorable" specs while losing the one thing that says what the analysis ran on: `burst_gs` (`bur_files`, 25 other controls), `sm_image_mle` (`sel_files`, `sel_irf_files`, 22), `img_pixel_mle` (same two, 17), `tttr_lut_tools` (`files`, 11), `clsm_generator` (`sel_lifetime_files`, 10), `img_calibration` (`sel_irf_files`, 9), `burst_irf_bg` / `ptu_alex_creator` / `tttr_splitter` (5 each) and `batch_analysis` (2). For a batch tool the file list *is* the analysis. Let a `custom` section opt into state by declaring its key in a small allow-list (`path_list`, and `region_list` once `RegionCollection` has a JSON form) with the state key taken from `target`, or add an explicit `stateful: true` flag to `CustomSection` — either way the collector must stop claiming coverage it does not have.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **`math/datatools.py` off numba — all nine kernels, and all nine bit-exact.** These are the interleaved-spectrum operations (`elte2`, `ere2`, `e1ti2`, `e1tn`, `invert_interleaved`) plus `minmax`, `discriminate`, `histogram1D` and `distance_between_gaussian`. The spectrum ones are exactly the class the fit profile caught numba's dispatcher sitting *above*: they work on `2 * n_components`-element arrays, where the write position `k` is the affine index `i * n2 + j`, so the doubly-nested loop is an `np.outer` whose Cartesian product already lands in C order. Verified bit-for-bit (`max|diff| = 0.0`) against the numba originals over 300 random cases each.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **Four more files off numba, and one of them was never compiled in the first place.** `math/reaction/_reaction.py` carried *two byte-identical copies* of the Gillespie SSA loop behind a `_HAVE_NUMBA` switch — and the numba one was `@nb.jit(forceobj=True)`, i.e. **object mode**, because the loop calls Python propensity callables and draws from `numpy.random`. Nothing in it was ever compiled; the switch chose between the same interpreted code reached directly and reached through a dispatcher. Collapsed to one function, no behaviour change by construction. `math/statistics.py::kl` (no callers anywhere, kept as public API rather than deleted) and the two interval fillers, `fluorescence/burst/utils.py::_fill_intervals` and `math/signal.py::_fill_gaps_helper`, are now **difference arrays** — `+1` at each start, `-1` at each stop, running sum — which is one pass over the output whatever the interval count, where the loop of slice assignments was one pass *per interval* and a burst search returns tens of thousands. Both OR their mask in rather than assigning over it, so values already set survive; the parity harness seeds the array with random `True`s precisely to catch an overwrite, and also feeds overlapping intervals, which the running-sum form handles and a naive `np.put` would not. 300 random cases each against the numba originals: `kl` agrees to 5.7e-14, both fillers **exactly**, empty inputs included.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **`fluorescence/general.py` is numba-free, and the port found a bug and a bad benchmark.** Eight kernels: six were one-line expressions (`distance_to_fret_efficiency`, `fret_efficiency_to_distance`, `rate_constant_to_lifetime`, `distance_to_fret_rate_constant`, `fret_induced_donor_decay`, `lifetime_to_fret_efficiency`) called with arrays from already-vectorised code; two were real loops. `_fast_convolve_loop` becomes an outer product binned with `bincount`, keeping its **right-closed** bins (`searchsorted(edges, v) - 1`, where a value equal to `edges[0]` is *dropped*) rather than `np.histogram`, whose left-closed bins disagree exactly at the edges — and the smallest product the caller feeds in is `edges[0]` by construction, so that difference is reachable. Verified against **committed fixtures generated from the numba originals** (`test/data/numba_parity/general_kernels.npz`, 40 random cases per kernel plus the edge cases), not against numba at test time: a live comparison would evaporate as a *skip that reads like a pass* the day numba leaves, which is the mdtraj lesson.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **Retiring numba from `chisurf/`, and the measurement that decides how.** 157 JIT kernels across 44 files, opened as a shrinking tracker (`test/numba_import_allowlist.txt` + `test/test_numba_seam.py`, the pyqtgraph-seam shape). The goal is stated honestly as **"`chisurf/` imports numba nowhere"**, not "the dependency is gone": `modules/quest` (20 kernels) and `modules/imp-tricks` (188) still declare it and `build-extensions` installs both, so numba stays in the solved environment until those follow. Its own footprint is **2 packages** (numba + llvmlite, 138 → 140 in a chisurf-shaped solve) — the reasons to remove it are the 229.5 ms GUI-thread JIT stall, the `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` pool that latches and makes `pytest test/fio` fail as a directory, `fastmath` folding away an `isfinite` guard, and no Pyodide story.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **Spot finding and lifetime fitting were one 897-line function, and the fit re-segmented behind the preview** — new [PRD-92](prds/prd-92.md) (draft), registered in the [PRD index](prds/index.md). `sm_image_mle` segments, measures, gathers photons and fits in one core, and `fit_molecules` calls `segment_molecules` *itself*: `segmentation_preview()` returns exactly the labels the fit will use, and the fit ignores them and derives a second segmentation, which agrees only for as long as every setting reaches both paths. Nothing persists the regions, so a segmentation cannot be reviewed, corrected, compared between parameter sets or produced by anything else — and none of the detection the tree grew after this plugin was written (`blob_log`/`blob_dog` and their scale space, `difference_of_gaussians`, `white_tophat`, `img_tracking`'s à-trous multiscale product) can feed the fit. The PRD splits it into a `spot_finder` plugin that writes its regions into the `.pto` and a renamed `region_mle` that fits the regions it is handed. Scoping found the one decision that cannot be deferred: **a table of `regionprops` scalars cannot say which photons belong to a region** — the fit reaches them through `prop.coords` → `clsm[0][r][c].tttr_indices`, one pixel at a time — so the persisted artifact must be a *pair*, an `image_data` label raster joined to the scalar table by a `label` column, and the table takes the burst-companion merge-by-position rule (one row per region including the ones the fit skipped, sentinel row never a missing row). No new writer is needed: `analysis_path.write_tables` already takes `artifact_kind`/`operation_type`/`row_grain`. Adds a 3-deep photons → regions → fits chain to [PRD-88](prds/prd-88.md)'s matrix, and the acceptance test is that the split reproduces today's per-region parameters to the last significant figure.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **`numexpr` retired: its one expression is a Numba kernel, 22× faster** ([build/env](workflows/build-and-env.md)). The whole dependency existed for a single line in the dye-diffusion quenching code — `ne.evaluate('sum(k_quench * collided,axis=1)')` — plus an `ne.set_num_threads()` at import. The replacement reduces each frame's row on its own thread and never materialises the `(n_frames, n_atoms)` product, which for a long trajectory against a whole protein's quenching atoms is the largest array in the calculation: on 200 000 × 400, **634.7 ms → 29.2 ms** (plain NumPy is 316.7 ms). It is also the *more* accurate of the two — numexpr accumulated in float32 because `k_quench` is float32.

Running the same headless bootstrap the agent layer already uses (`ensure_experiments_registered`) takes it to **43**, and the error now lists what is available.

findings.message: duplicate log bullet
findings.source: * **ChiMOL sees through a surface: `transparency` and `two_sided_lighting`** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The first and fourth names on the settings worklist, and the two `preset ligand_sites` had been reporting as skipped. **PyMOL counts transparency where chimol stores alpha, and they run opposite ways** -- `transparency 0` is opaque, `alpha 1` is -- so `SettingSpec` gained `stored`/`shown` transforms and the complement is declared once rather than kept as two numbers that must agree. A guardrail asserts every transforming spec round-trips. `unset transparency` restores chimol's shipped 0.15, not PyMOL's 0: `unset` restores *the* default, and changing what this program ships is a config migration, not a settings entry. 70 registered settings, each read by code.

findings.source: * **ebFRET's MATLAB GUI ported onto emtk as the `burst_ebfret` plugin.** A plain port of `junk/ebFRET`: the MainWindow's panels, menus (File/Analysis/View incl. findings.source: `byring` uses **every** ring, not the planar ones: it is a question about connectivity, and a proline is as much a ring as a phenylalanine. One trap taken from the source — PyMOL *clears* the mask before its ring finder runs (`std::fill_n` in `SELE_RING`), so an atom in no ring is dropped: `byring (name CA)` is 15 atoms (the prolines), not 177.

findings.source: * **Correction: the missing ligand ring is not a gap against PyMOL** ([pymol-parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md), [molecular viewer guide](../docs/guides/44_molecular_viewer.md)). Earlier today the pi-interaction work recorded "an untemplated ligand's aromatic ring is not found; PyMOL, with its chemistry pass, does find those". Checking the source afterwards shows that is wrong in both halves. `ObjectMoleculeGetAtomGeometry` runs its cross products only for **three** neighbours — two neighbours detect *linear* and nothing else — and `InferChemFromBonds` consumes bond orders that a PDB ligand does not carry, so PyMOL misses the same rings for the same reason.

findings.source: The load-bearing part is none of the three finders but **formal charge**: a salt bridge is "two heavy atoms of opposite formal charge within 5 Å" and a PDB file carries no charges. PyMOL fills them in from nomenclature (`assign_pdb_known_residue`) and the table is transcribed with its asymmetries intact, because they *are* the correctness — one oxygen of a carboxylate, one nitrogen of a guanidinium (`NH2` explicitly pinned to zero), and **a plain `HIS` is neutral** since only `HIP`/`HISP`/`HISH` are charged. Charging both halves of a carboxylate double-counts every bridge; guessing histidine's protonation is a decision PyMOL declines to make.

findings.source: * **`ray` framed the widget instead of the viewport** ([pymol-parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md), [molecular viewer guide](../docs/guides/44_molecular_viewer.md)). Standing item 0c, open since 2026-08-06 and inherited by every headless screenshot of chimol: `orient` then `ray` put the molecule off-centre and small. Neither the camera nor the tracer was wrong — `ray` with no size defaulted to the **whole GL widget**, while the viewport draws the scene into what is left after the panel's column and the sequence viewer's band. The trace therefore covered a wider field than the screen and centred the molecule in it. Measured on a 998x583 widget: **59 %** of the traced width against **70 %** on screen, displaced towards the panel. PyMOL's default is taken "from the current viewpoint", which is that rectangle; its second rule was also wrong here — given one dimension the other must "preserve the current aspect ratio", and chimol used a fixed 4:3. `MolView.scene_pixel_size()` now answers it in device pixels, so a default trace and a screenshot match on a retina display. After the fix the traced bounding box agrees with the viewport's to **0.003 of the frame** in every direction.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.source: * **The mutagenesis wizard previews rotamers as *states*, PyMOL's way, and that is what made it fast** ([pymol-parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md), [molecular viewer guide](../docs/guides/44_molecular_viewer.md)). The wizard's first form rebuilt the residue inside the source object on every step: correct, undoable, and **2.2 s per step** on a 1363-atom protein, because rebuilding a residue runs `set_structure` over the whole molecule and re-bakes ambient occlusion for 1349 atoms that did not move. The reported symptom was "super slow", and the suggested fix was numba; the profile says the arithmetic was never the cost — building all 81 rotamers of the largest residue is **28 ms** and scoring them **97 ms**. PyMOL's `do_library` removes the cost by design: one object called `mutation`, `cmd.create(obj, frag, 1, state)` per rotamer, and stepping is a state change. Ported: **build a target 2881 → 320 ms, step a rotamer 2172 → 32 ms**, same Python. `Clear`/`Done` became a delete instead of a restore, since the source is never touched.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

Water may bridge two halves, be excluded, or be the whole question (the wire). ChimeraX does not name a network either.

findings.source: **The clash check is PyMOL's, and it is not a command there** — it is the bump check inside the mutagenesis wizard. Transcribed from `Sculpt.cpp`: the hb-overlap allowances (without which every hydrogen bond reports as a clash), the exclusion arms (1-2 and 1-3 out, a 1-4 pair scored but *never drawn* — `SculptCGOBump` is called only in the unexcluded arm), and the green-to-red colour. The radii are PyMOL's `ElementTable`, not the reader's force-field radii: on 148L that is 15 deep overlaps against 862, which is the measurement that decided the design.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: **Mutation is PyMOL's loop with PyMOL's data.** `do_library` — fragment onto the backbone, one state per rotamer, bump-check each, start on the least strained — with the fragments and the rotamer library *generated* from the reference checkout rather than re-derived, the same pattern the 547 space groups use. The fit residual is absorbed as a translation onto CA so it lands in the N-CA-CB angle instead of stretching the CA-CB bond, and the side chain is scored with its own bonds or a tryptophan strains 60 before touching anything. Validated by the identity rebuild: every residue of 148L mutated into itself, the library's best rotamer landing **0.50 Å** from the deposited side chain on average, 31 of 33 within 1 Å.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: **And mutation got PyMOL's simplest GUI**: the wizard panel. `Wizard.get_panel()` is rows of `[code, label, action]` — a banner, buttons, pop-ups — drawn under the object list, with the prompt in the top-left of the scene; three codes, and every wizard PyMOL ships is built from them. That vocabulary is transcribed, and the mutagenesis wizard is its first user, because choosing a rotamer means looking at each one. It previews **in place** rather than as states of a separate object (milliseconds per rebuild, one fewer object to explain) and keeps a copy of the original rows so `Clear` and `Done` put the residue back atom for atom. The prompt sits below the sequence strip: at the window's own top edge it lands on the residue numbers, which only a screenshot shows. Open: the backbone-dependent rotamer library (written, not shipped), and PyMOL's other four wizards, which is why the Wizard menu lists one entry rather than five with four disabled.

It previews **in place** rather than as states of a separate object (milliseconds per rebuild, one fewer object to explain) and keeps a copy of the original rows so `Clear` and `Done` put the residue back atom for atom. The prompt sits below the sequence strip: at the window's own top edge it lands on the residue numbers, which only a screenshot shows. Open: the backbone-dependent rotamer library (written, not shipped), and PyMOL's other four wizards, which is why the Wizard menu lists one entry rather than five with four disabled.

findings.source: **The marker.** PyMOL's indicator is three concentric filled squares at every selected *atom* — pink `(1.0, 0.2, 0.6)` at the full width, black at half, white in the middle — sized by `selection_width_scale * stick_radius / vScale` clamped to 3..10 px. chimol drew a thin ring at each *residue* in the shipped config's yellow, argued for as Chimera's outline: the middle of a ring is only covered when the marker is depth-tested against the geometry it hugs, this one is an overlay, and one point per residue had nothing to hug. Transcribed as one shader pass with PyMOL's own ratios, and carried to existing installs by display-config migration 10 — the default alone would have reached nobody, because a user's `chimol_display.json` is written once and never refreshed.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: **Menus.** Qt delivers a mouse move to a widget without `setMouseTracking(True)` only while a button is held, and the GL widget never set it — so no row highlight, no menu-entry highlight, and no hover-open. A submenu could only be opened by *clicking* it, and nothing ever told the panel the cursor had left, so they piled up. `InternalGui.mouse_move` was covered by tests and correct; the tests call it directly, and nothing called it in the app. On top of that, placement clamped a submenu into the window instead of flipping it to the other side — with the panel docked against the right edge, that put every submenu on top of its own parent. Both halves are now PyMOL's (`layer4/PopUp.cpp`, `layer1/Pop.cpp`): `PopPlaceChild`'s try-preferred-side-then-flip with an inherited `PlacementAffinity`, the child's first entry aligned with the row it hangs off, and the child freed as soon as the cursor is on another row. One deliberate difference: PyMOL waits `cChildDelay` (0.25 s) before closing, for sloppy mousing; chimol closes immediately, which is affordable only because the child sits adjacent to the row.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: Three things it turned on. PyMOL lists every symbol **twice**, cased and upper (`He` and `HE`), and that duplication is the useful part rather than noise: a PDB element column is written both ways, and a table that knows one spelling drops every metal in half the files there are -- to *nothing*, not to an error. An unknown symbol returns `None` and is **counted**, never defaulted, because a weight quietly missing a metal is the kind of wrong number that gets published. And the table is verified by **properties plus its size**: a truncated extraction is self-consistent and passes every spot check that falls inside it, so the count is asserted alongside the IUPAC values *and* a check that masses rise across a period -- which is what catches a dropped row pairing symbols with their neighbours' masses.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: `depth_cue` / `fog` / `fog_start` are PyMOL's and are **global**: both renderers read them. They were registered under `ray.*` from when only the tracer honoured them, so the prefix said something untrue. Moving them needed the loader extension the tracker predicted -- `DISPLAY_CONFIG_MIGRATIONS` can only change a *value* -- so `DISPLAY_CONFIG_KEY_MOVES` sits beside it, and **its rule is the mirror image**, which is the part worth remembering: a value migration moves what the user did *not* choose (it still equals the old default), a key move carries across what they *did*, and drops the old key either way so the section it left keeps no stale twin. They are `depth_cue.enabled` / `.start` / `.intensity`; config version 8 -> 9. Six tests, including one that asserts every move's destination is a key the package actually ships -- a move to a key that is not there writes a value nothing reads, which is worse than not moving it.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: pymol
findings.source: * **`silhouette` had two stores, so `set silhouette, on` could not exist** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The settings lived on the renderer's `PostProcess` object *and* in `_DISPLAY_CONFIG["silhouette"]`, read exactly once in `QtGLRenderer.__init__` -- so `lighting silhouette=on` moved the picture without touching the configuration, and the configuration was a start-up default no live change could reach. Registering the name against that store would have produced exactly the accepted-and-inert setting `surface_quality` turned out to be four times over. `PostProcess` reads the section through properties now: one store, read where it is used, so an already-constructed renderer sees a `set`. With that true the names are safe to register, and `silhouette`, `silhouette_thickness`, `depth_jump` and `silhouette_color` are.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: **The camera was following the frame, and only a growing structure showed it.** `_select_state_frame` recomputed the object's centre and radius from the frame on show, so the camera chased the current frame's centroid -- the scene centre swung 0 -> -21 -> +52 scene units over the biofilm's run and the substratum slid about beneath a film that was supposed to be growing off it. On a molecule the extent barely changes and it reads as a gentle wander, which is why it survived; it was also hiding half of what the trajectory demo teaches, since following the centroid removes exactly the translational drift `intra_fit` is there to remove. Not deleted, because for a molecule wandering across a box that behaviour is the useful one: it is `movie_recenter` (`camera.recenter_on_frame`), on by default, read from the config **where it is used** so a live `set` reaches an open viewer and there is no second store to leave stale. `set` is global as it is in PyMOL, so each demo that cares now states the value it wants. The first version of the test passed **vacuously** -- the centre is computed over all rows, not the visible ones, so a fixture whose particles never move cannot exercise re-centring at all; it needed a drift term.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: VMD
findings.source: * **ChiSurf reads and writes DCD itself, and it is faster than the C plugin** ([PRD-80](prds/prd-80.md)). First step of retiring mdtraj: `chisurf/core/fio/trajectory/dcd.py`, ported from VMD's `dcdplugin.c` — the **permissively licensed** (UIUC) C reference, not mdtraj's LGPL `.pyx` wrapper — to NumPy rather than a compiled extension, since ChiSurf is Cython-free. A frame is three contiguous `float32` blocks, so reading one is a `np.frombuffer`. On 2500 atoms × 200 frames: **write 22 ms and read 5 ms, against mdtraj's 34 ms and 14 ms** — one read plus a `frombuffer` per frame beats a `fread` per record.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: VMD
findings.source: **The unit cell is where this format bites.** Six values stored interleaved as `(A, gamma, B, beta, alpha, C)`, and as *cosines* in CHARMM/NAMD > 2.5 but as *degrees* in NAMD 2.5, with no flag to say which — a reader tells them apart by whether all three fall inside [-1, 1]. Both paths are covered, and the decodings were **mutation-tested**: swapping alpha/gamma, taking the lengths as values 0–2, and skipping the cosine branch are each caught. (A fourth mutation, `arccos` for `90 − asin`, is *not* caught and should not be — the two are the same identity; VMD prefers the latter only for its rounding at exactly 90°.)
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **`ray` was far darker than the viewport: a missing term, not a missing setting** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Reported as "way too dark, and the lighting does not correspond to the live view" — one fault, not two. PyMOL's traced brightness has **two** diffuse terms: `bright = ambient + direct*direct_cmp + lreflect*reflect_cmp`, where `direct_cmp = pow(surfnormal[2], power)` is the normal's z in *camera* space — so `direct` is a **headlight**, lighting whatever faces the viewer regardless of the lamps. chimol had only the lamp term, so its ceiling was `ambient + diffuse` = **0.59** against PyMOL's ~1.0. (The averaging over lights was already right: `lreflect` carries `reflect_scale`, commented in the source as "divide up the reflected light component over all lights".) Measured on 148L's cartoon against the GL viewport, same scene and camera: mean lit **35.5 → 50.3**, viewport **51.1** — from 30 % below it to within 2 %. `direct` (0.45) and `power` (1.0) registered under PyMOL's names and defaults (`SettingInfo.h` 8, 11); new config keys, so no migration.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **`ray` looked slow, and it was compiling, not tracing** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Reported as "1f5n takes more than 10 s". The trace is **0.4–0.6 s** for that structure at 638×291 2×2, and 0.46 s end-to-end through the command, thread and PNG write in a fresh process. The 10–33 s is **numba compiling the tracer**, cached under `~/.chisurf/cache/<module>_<contenthash>/` — and the hash is over the source, so *every* edit to `raytracer.py` or `bvh.py` discards the cache and the next `ray` pays a full recompile. Measured: **33.5 s** immediately after a kernel signature changed, **0.46 s** in the next fresh process; a fresh install pays it once. With nothing said that reads as "ray is slow", and the number reported back is the compile — so `ray` now announces the compile when `_jit_trace` has no signatures yet, and reports elapsed time in its "wrote" message either way.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **A cartoon casts a shadow now, and the WebGL viewer is read out** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `ray_shadow` did nothing on the display chimol and PyMOL both start with: the shadow query walked a **sphere-only** tree, so a cartoon — zero spheres — reported every point fully lit, and a helix lying across another did not darken it. PyMOL shadows every primitive. The second tree was an optimisation from when a shadow ray cost a sweep of the whole scene; with the BVH it is one more descent of a tree that already exists, **so the fix deletes code rather than adding it** — one tree for both ray kinds, and `skip` becomes the hit primitive's unified index, finally correct for a triangle as well as a sphere. Cost on 148L at 320×240 2×2: cartoon 0.05 → 0.07 s, sticks 0.04 → 0.08 s, surface 0.07 → 0.12 s — 40–70 % more, from a base 100× faster than this morning. Checked for self-shadow acne, the failure mode this class of change has: none, and the difference sits in the crevices between surface lobes and under the ribbons, which is where a cast shadow belongs. 91 passed.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.source: * **The WebGL viewer (`junk/ngl`) is read out, and its checkout is deleted.** Surveyed the whole tree, not only the shaders. What it was consulted for is captured: the five shader techniques are transcribed into the tracker, and one of the five was **measured and rejected** (impostors buy ~1 ms on an ordinary molecule). Everything else duplicates an authority chimol already has and the authority is better — its representations (`rocket`, `unitcell`, `slice`, `hyperball`), colour schemes (hydrophobicity, occupancy, partial charge, B-factor) and measurements all exist in PyMOL under names chimol is *required* to match, so taking them from NGL would mean implementing the right feature under the wrong name and defaults. Two things neither PyMOL nor ChimeraX has are written down so dropping the checkout does not lose them: an EDT-based solvent-excluded surface (a third algorithm again — PyMOL's is the one to match), and a flat spatial hash that `geometry/neighbors.py` already implements. **PyMOL stays the authority on behaviour, ChimeraX on rendering quality; NGL was only ever the third opinion on shaders.** The 1.0 GB checkout is **deleted**, and two things were done so the deletion sticks and costs nothing: the tracker now carries the upstream URL and the exact commit everything was read from (`60be69b5`), since the shader notes cite paths inside it; and `junk/clone.sh` — which re-clones every reference tree and would have silently restored it on the next run — carries the decision instead of the clone line.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **The viewport had no depth cue, and PyMOL's settings for it were pointed at the tracer** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `depth_cue`, `fog` and `fog_start` are *global* in PyMOL — `SceneSetFog` applies them to the viewport and the tracer follows unless `ray_trace_fog`/`ray_trace_fog_start` override, which is why those two names exist. chimol registered all three against `ray.*` and applied them only to the tracer, so the interactive view had **no depth cue at all** and the traced image disagreed with the viewport it reproduces. The shader was already written for it: `fogDensity`, `fogColor`, the uniform lookup and the fragment `mix` were all in place, and `self._fog_density = 0.0` in `__init__` was **the only assignment in the tree** — a complete feature held off by one initialiser, and the fourth thing this session that was built and unreachable.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: Both halves transcribed rather than invented. **Shape:** PyMOL's fog is *linear between two planes*, `fog = (g_Fog_end + eye_pos.z) * g_Fog_scale` in `data/shaders/default.vs`, a **visibility** with scale `1/(end − start)`; chimol's shader had `1 − exp(−density·|viewPos|)`, a different curve that makes `fog_start` mean nothing. **Planes:** `FogStart = (back − front)·fog_start + front`, `FogEnd = FogStart + (back − FogStart)/fog` for `fog` in (0,1) else `back`, with front/back fitted **around the scene** (camera distance ± target radius) rather than the camera's far plane — the identical distinction the tracer's fog fix turned on, where getting it wrong fogged every pixel 24–69 % with none left unfogged. Defaults are PyMOL's: `depth_cue` on, `fog` 1.0, `fog_start` 0.45.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **Silhouettes were built and unusable: switching them on deleted the sequence strip and moved the molecule** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The tracker named the render-to-texture scaffolding as the *next task*; it has been there for some time with silhouettes on top of it — another stated gap with a shelf life. What was true is that nobody could have used it. Three defects, all where the offscreen pass meets the rest of the frame, all invisible to the suite because nothing rendered a *window* with an effect on: (1) `_render_overlay` paints with QPainter, which targets the **widget's** framebuffer rather than the bound one, and it ran *before* the composite, so the blit erased the chrome — the strip lost **53 %** of its ink (the two early-return paths in `paintGL` already had the right order; only the path that draws a molecule did not); (2) the offscreen buffer took the window's full height while the direct path reserves a band for the strip, so the scene rendered centred in a taller frame and visibly shifted, and the blit covered the band too; (3) a window that has not been laid out built a **1-pixel-wide** framebuffer — the same `scene_width` floor that once told the camera the window was thirty times taller than wide — so the composite blitted a one-pixel column and **the molecule disappeared**. The effect passes now decline below `_MIN_MEASURABLE_SCENE`.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.source: * **Every ChiMOL frame rebuilt the whole scene, through a colour query: surface 82 ms → 4.25 ms** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `paintGL` → `_render_overlay` → `_refresh_gui_state` → `get_residue_colors` → **`_build_scene_for_current_object`**. The sequence strip has no signal telling it that `color`/`spectrum`/`ss` ran, so it re-reads the residue colours every frame — reasonable — but the only way to get them ran the entire scene builder: with a surface shown, a density grid, marching cubes, gradients and ambient occlusion **sixty times a second**. 148L at 1280×860: surface **82.12 → 4.25 ms** (12 → 235 fps), cartoon 28.34 → 4.12, spheres 17.34 → 4.94, sticks 11.61 → 3.91. The colour half is split out as `_recompute_colors_per_ca`, which is all `get_residue_colors` calls now.

findings.source: * **Shader techniques surveyed from a WebGL viewer, none taken yet** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `junk/ngl/src/shader/` read for *how* while PyMOL stays the authority on *what*. The headline: ChiMOL draws spheres as impostors only past 20 000 atoms, so an ordinary molecule gets tessellated sticks — **33 216 triangles on 148L** for what is a few hundred capped cylinders — where a cylinder impostor ray-casts them exactly from one quad, faster and without facets at any zoom. Four smaller ones, each a handful of lines: interior colouring so a clipped surface reads as solid rather than hollow (the same `gl_FrontFacing` hook `two_sided_lighting` already added), opaque back faces as the cheap half of order-independent transparency, SDF glyphs for labels that survive zoom, and a matrix-scale helper so an impostor radius survives a scaled transform. Recorded with what each buys, in the rendering section.

findings.source: * **`ray` was 143–651× slower than it needed to be; every ray tested every primitive** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The tracer had no acceleration structure: each sample intersected every sphere and every triangle in the scene, for every transparency layer. A cartoon is 39 252 triangles and a solvent surface 51 748, so a publication-sized render — 1024×768, 2×2 samples — cost **195 s**. It now costs **0.30 s**. Measured on 148L at 320×240 2×2: cartoon 19.12 s → 0.126 s (151×), sticks 8.96 → 0.062 (144×), surface 35.00 → 0.198 (177×), lines 51.11 → 0.152 (337×). A binned-SAH BVH in `renderer/bvh.py`, with spheres and triangles in one index space so a mixed scene is one tree and one descent.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: **The picture is unchanged, and that was differenced rather than assumed.** cartoon, sticks and surface are **bit-identical**, every pixel. `spheres` (3.6 % of pixels) and `lines` (0.03 %) differ because the tree exposed a defect it did not cause: the shadow query returned **whichever occluder came first in the array**, so contact-shadow softness depended on scene build order. PyMOL takes the nearest, and only when the decay is on — `nearest_shadow = (shadow_decay != _0)`, `layer1/Ray.cpp` — because the decay is a function of occluder distance. All 2 788 changed pixels are **brighter, none darker**, which is what the nearest occluder implies under `occlusion = 1 − exp(−(t − decay_range)·decay)` and is how the change was confirmed to be that one change alone. A second defect fell out beside it: the hit primitive was passed as the sphere to skip **without checking it was a sphere**, so a triangle hit stopped one sphere from casting — invisible except on a mixed scene, which is what a wireframe is.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.source: * **Numba is required across ChiMOL; the unexercised NumPy twins are gone** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Ten modules carried `_HAVE_NUMBA` with a pure-NumPy sibling behind it. Nothing ran those siblings while numba was installed -- which is exactly how the ray tracer's twin came to be **silently broken**: the transparency work landed in both, the NumPy one referenced a parameter it did not take, and every test still passed. A fallback nobody runs is not a safety net but an untested branch. ~600 lines removed, along with the `except Exception: pass` handlers that quietly downgraded a jit failure to a slower path.

findings.source: * **`surface_quality` was three defects wearing one name** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Flagged as a units wart -- PyMOL takes a level, chimol a grid spacing -- and each measurement found something worse underneath. **It is not a different quantity**: `RepSurfaceSetSettings` shows the level *selects* a point separation in Angstrom, which is what chimol stores; the eight levels and four base separations are transcribed, the bases registered because the table reads them. **Then the level did nothing** -- levels -3 to 1 moved 148L from 26 286 to 27 238 vertices, 3.6 % across an eightfold request, because `max_dim` caps the grid at 96 samples/axis and *rescales the spacing to fit*. **Then the reason turned out to be worse**: `_all_atom_coords` is in scene units (Angstrom x 10) and the spacing was passed through as if it were too, so `0.8` asked for **0.08 A** and the cap clamped it back. The spacing had never had a measurable effect; `max_dim` was making the whole decision. `add_volume` already converts -- one path forgot what its neighbour remembers.
findings.acceptance: Remove this finding and its baseline record; final baseline must be empty.

findings.source: * **ChiMOL sees through a surface: `transparency` and `two_sided_lighting`** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The first and fourth names on the settings worklist, and the two `preset ligand_sites` had been reporting as skipped. **PyMOL counts transparency where chimol stores alpha, and they run opposite ways** -- `transparency 0` is opaque, `alpha 1` is -- so `SettingSpec` gained `stored`/`shown` transforms and the complement is declared once rather than kept as two numbers that must agree. A guardrail asserts every transforming spec round-trips. `unset transparency` restores chimol's shipped 0.15, not PyMOL's 0: `unset` restores *the* default, and changing what this program ships is a config migration, not a settings entry. 70 registered settings, each read by code.

findings.source: * **The framing correction ran on a window that did not exist** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Five tests in `test_camera_framing.py` were red at HEAD, every one by a factor of **exactly 30**. `scene_width()` subtracts the internal panel's 220-pixel column and clamps the remainder to 1, so a never-laid-out `MolView` (100x30) reported an aspect of **1/30** — and PyMOL's portrait correction, given a window "thirty times taller than wide", put the camera thirty times too far away. `_aspect()` now returns 1.0 below a 16-pixel viewport: an aspect measured off a one-pixel column is not a measurement, and there is nothing to correct until there is a window. Two guardrail tests, one for each direction — the unlaid-out case frames square, a genuine 400x900 portrait still corrects. Found while running the suite for the polar-contact work; unrelated to it, fixed in the same change.

findings.source: **The cutoff is a curve, not a number** — the donor-acceptor limit slides with the A-D-H angle from `h_bond_cutoff_center` (3.6 Å head-on) to `h_bond_cutoff_edge` (3.2 Å at 63°), and the two names read backwards from what they do. Two more details invisible without the C++: the virtual hydrogen sits at **1.0 Å**, not the real X-H bond length (`FindBestDonorH` adds a *unit* vector), and an atom with no neighbours aims its hydrogen **straight at the acceptor**, which is how PyMOL finds water-mediated contacts in a hydrogen-less PDB rather than a bug to fix.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: Donors and acceptors need bond orders a PDB does not carry. PyMOL fills that with a hard-coded double-bond table for standard residues plus valence arithmetic for the rest; chimol already had the equivalent of the first in the `h_add` residue template, so a templated atom is typed from it (which is what keeps a backbone carbonyl an acceptor and not a donor) and an untemplated one from expected valence with geometry read off its bond angles. **Measured against reality**: on the fully hydrogenated `hGBP1_closed.pdb`, asking with and without hydrogens gives 735 vs 803 contacts sharing 729 pairs — **99.2 % recall** with every hydrogen invented. On 148L, 234 contacts in 0.02 s, over 40 of them the i→i−4 bonds that define an α-helix. One deliberate deviation: PyMOL invents an amide hydrogen for **proline**, which has none.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: - **Click and box select carry PyMOL's *action*, not a modifier.** `view.py` gained `_apply_selection_indices(indices, modifiers, mode)` which merges by action code — `toggle` (`+/-`), `add` (`+Box`), `subtract` (`-Box`), `set` (`Sele`), `pick` (`PkAt`) — and `handle_mouse_click`/`handle_rect_selection` now take the action. `mouse_modes.py::click_action_of` resolves the `single_*` cells, because PyMOL distinguishes the press action (`l,none` → `rota`) from the click action (`single_left,none` → `+/-`). `qtgl.py` therefore records the press and decides on release: a click toggles the picked residue, `sele` sets, `pkat` picks without touching the selection, and an empty-space click leaves the selection alone (PyMOL's "no atom found nearby"). Tests: `test/test_mouse_selection.py` (7) plus the mouse-mode table tests.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: - **`sele` is a real, always-last object entry.** It is pinned to the bottom of the in-viewport object panel (PyMOL draws its selection object below every molecule and the `all` header), has no on/off state of its own, and its A/S/H/L/C menus address `sele`. Because PyMOL's `sele` *always exists and is what the mouse writes to*, `cmd/selection.py` resolves the bare name to the viewer's live residue selection (`_selected_residues_atom_mask`) whenever no stored entry exists, so `show sticks, sele` reaches exactly the clicked/boxed residues; a stored entry still wins. Named selections now also resolve as atoms inside expressions (`sele_parser.Evaluator(named_selections=...)`), so `mysel and resi 10` is meaningful.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: - **The sequence strip is PyMOL's Seeker.** A click toggles a residue, shift-click extends the previous drag gesture additively, ctrl-click toggles and keeps the rest, a ctrl-drag merges the range, and a double-click on blank sequence area clears the selection. `internal_gui.py` threads `modifiers`/`double` through `mouse_press`, keeps a `_seq_anchor` for the shift continuation, and emits the whole selected set because the mirror into the 3-D view replaces rather than merges. Tests in `test_internal_gui.py` (toggle, shift-extend, ctrl-merge, ctrl-drag, blank double-click, `sele` row pinned/no-on-off/buttons-address-`sele`).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **Rebuilt the ChiMOL `cmd` layer as a declarative, signature-driven command language (PyMOL-parity architecture).** Ported PyMOL's four-piece design to Python introspection: a `@command` decorator + `collect_commands` registry with a minimal-unique-prefix `Shortcut` index (`registry.py`), and a central comma/keyword/bracket/quote-aware tokenizer + `inspect.signature` binder with annotation-driven coercion and `raw1`/`raw2` verbatim-tail modes (`argparse2.py`, `selection_types.Selection`). Migrated **every** command mixin (loader/rendering/selection/measurements/editing/animation/exporting/lifecycle + base `help`/`quit`/`exit`) from the old `_cmd_x(args: List[str])` + `_mixin_commands()` handlers to typed `@command` methods, so adding a command is now writing one annotated method and parsing/keyword-args/coercion/Python-API come free (`align a, b, cutoff=3, cycles=10` binds natively). Removed the dual-dispatch adapter — `base.py:do()` resolves solely through the registry — and deleted the dead `cmd/core.py` (2556-line legacy monolith) and never-registered `cmd/rmf.py`. External callers (`cli.py`, `command_dock.py`) now read the command list via the new `Cmd.command_names()`. Added `count_atoms` and `set_name` as the payoff. **Fixed a latent Python-3.11+ bug** in `sele_parser.py`: the per-token patterns carried inline `(?i)` flags that, once joined with `|`, landed mid-expression and made `TOKEN_REGEX` fail to compile — silently breaking every selection evaluation (color/select/alter/remove/align on real structures); hoisted to a single `re.IGNORECASE`. Full chimol suite now green with **nothing excluded** (136 passed), where alignment/editing/selection-grammar previously had to be skipped. See [plugins/profiles/chimol.md](/plugins/profiles/chimol.md).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **ChiMOL `cmd` gained PyMOL's core viewing/transform commands.** Added `turn`, `move`, `clip`, `rotate` and `translate` (RenderingMixin), the most-used PyMOL commands that were missing and that complement the new trackball navigation. Camera commands go cmd → `MolView` → `qtgl` renderer, all built on the rotation-matrix camera: `turn <x|y|z>, <angle>` left-multiplies the view rotation about a screen axis (Rodrigues); `move <x|y|z>, <dist>` pans (x/y) or dollies (z); `clip <near|far|slab|move>, <dist>` shifts the clip planes. `rotate <x|y|z>, <angle> [, sel]` and `translate [x,y,z] [, sel]` build a rigid transform and call `apply_transform_to_object` — verified `rotate x, 90` gives PyMOL's +90° ((0,1,0)→(0,0,1)) on the real `arr @ R^T` convention; fixed `MockViewer.apply_transform_to_object` (was `arr @ R`, missing the transpose) to match and gave it `turn`/`move`/`clip` stubs so the commands are testable headless. New `test_cmd_viewing.py` (**4**): registration, rotate/translate math, and camera-command dispatch. Chimol suite **89 passed**; lint net down (`cmd/rendering.py` 34→0 via cleanup, `qtgl`/`view` unchanged). More of PyMOL's surface (`create`, `set_name`, `dss`, `origin`, `count_atoms`, `save`, `run`) remains for follow-up. See [plugins/profiles/chimol.md](/plugins/profiles/chimol.md).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **ChiMOL navigation now matches PyMOL: virtual trackball + PyMOL button mapping.** The camera was a turntable (fixed azimuth/elevation about world Z/X), so it couldn't roll or rotate about an arbitrary screen axis and felt unlike PyMOL. Extracted PyMOL's `SceneMouse.cpp` behaviour via subagent and reimplemented in `qtgl.py`: the camera orientation is now a 3×3 world→camera rotation matrix; **left-drag is a virtual trackball** (project prev/cur cursor onto a sphere of radius `0.45·min(W,H)`, rotate about `cross(n_prev,n_cur)` with `mouse_scale`=1.3 and roll-damping `1/(1+|axis.z|)`, left-multiply the rotation, SVD re-orthonormalise to prevent drift); **middle-drag pans** (unchanged, already the correct `depth·2tan(fov/2)/H` pixel→world scale); **right-drag dollies** (`Δ = dy/400·max(5,distance)`) while a right-*click* still opens the context menu. Camera right/up/forward now come straight from the rotation rows, and the 18-float view state stores the rotation in slots 0–8 (PyMOL's convention) with a legacy fallback that reads the old elevation/azimuth in slots 10–11; `raytracer._camera_from_view_state` decodes the same, so the offscreen raytrace and the GL view stay consistent (verified: GL camera origin/forward derivation matches the raytracer's exactly, and a default-view raytrace of 148L renders upright). `reset_view(distance,elevation,azimuth)` keeps its signature (builds the matrix internally) so callers are unchanged. Trackball math unit-checked (orthonormal, ~0.4°/px, no drift over 200 drags); chimol suite **85 passed**; no new lint (`qtgl.py` 56→56, `raytracer.py` 23→23). The GL feel (rotation direction) can't be verified headlessly; it follows PyMOL's formula. See [plugins/profiles/chimol.md](/plugins/profiles/chimol.md).

findings.source: * **ChiMOL navigation now matches PyMOL: virtual trackball + PyMOL button mapping.** The camera was a turntable (fixed azimuth/elevation about world Z/X), so it couldn't roll or rotate about an arbitrary screen axis and felt unlike PyMOL. Extracted PyMOL's `SceneMouse.cpp` behaviour via subagent and reimplemented in `qtgl.py`: the camera orientation is now a 3×3 world→camera rotation matrix; **left-drag is a virtual trackball** (project prev/cur cursor onto a sphere of radius `0.45·min(W,H)`, rotate about `cross(n_prev,n_cur)` with `mouse_scale`=1.3 and roll-damping `1/(1+|axis.z|)`, left-multiply the rotation, SVD re-orthonormalise to prevent drift); **middle-drag pans** (unchanged, already the correct `depth·2tan(fov/2)/H` pixel→world scale); **right-drag dollies** (`Δ = dy/400·max(5,distance)`) while a right-*click* still opens the context menu. Camera right/up/forward now come straight from the rotation rows, and the 18-float view state stores the rotation in slots 0–8 (PyMOL's convention) with a legacy fallback that reads the old elevation/azimuth in slots 10–11; `raytracer._camera_from_view_state` decodes the same, so the offscreen raytrace and the GL view stay consistent (verified: GL camera origin/forward derivation matches the raytracer's exactly, and a default-view raytrace of 148L renders upright). `reset_view(distance,elevation,azimuth)` keeps its signature (builds the matrix internally) so callers are unchanged. Trackball math unit-checked (orthonormal, ~0.4°/px, no drift over 200 drags); chimol suite **85 passed**; no new lint (`qtgl.py` 56→56, `raytracer.py` 23→23). The GL feel (rotation direction) can't be verified headlessly; it follows PyMOL's formula. See [plugins/profiles/chimol.md](/plugins/profiles/chimol.md).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: PyMOL
findings.source: * **ChiMOL cartoon no longer twists — PyMOL-style ribbon orientation.** The cartoon rendered helices as jagged "twisted tape" because the ribbon orientation used the raw per-residue carbonyl direction (`C - O`), which is noisy and, in a helix, spins around the axis with each residue. Rebuilt the orientation pipeline against PyMOL's `RepCartoon.cpp` (extracted via subagent): (1) `_build_trace_ups` now uses the **peptide-plane normal** `normalize((N−C)×(N−O))` (PyMOL's `RepCartoonGeneratePASS1`) instead of `C−O`; (2) a new `_refine_orientations` applies PyMOL's three anti-twist passes before spline sampling — **round helices** (helix orientation = `normalize(axis × tangent)` with `axis` a running CA-difference sum, so the oval circles a smooth axis), **flat sheets** (4-cycle 3-point box average of orientations across each β-strand so it shares one up-vector), and **refine-normals** (force ⊥ tangent, propagate sign forward to kill 180° flips). Verified by offscreen raytraced renders of 148L (helices go from broken twisted tape to smooth spiralling ribbons) and 1rtd (proper mixed α/β). Cross-section dimensions already matched PyMOL (oval 0.25×1.35, rect 0.4×1.4, loop r=0.2). `test_geometry_vectorized` + fallback-render suites **12 passed**; `cartoon.py` lint unchanged (43→43). See [plugins/profiles/chimol.md](/plugins/profiles/chimol.md).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: origin
findings.source: * **Parameter detail popup made compact: 650x520 -> 414x120 px.** `FittingParameterDetailPopup` laid every control on its own full-width row, so a popup meant to sit next to the parameter it edits covered most of the fit window. Rows are now merged where they read together — name + link state + Link…/Unlink in the header, Value + Fixed on one row, Enable-bounds + Low + High on one row — the `Prior` group box became an inline `Prior:` label + radio row (one less frame and two less rows of padding), the redundant "Click outside to close" hint is gone (the popup is a `Qt.Popup`; that is its documented behaviour), spin boxes are width-capped, and spacing dropped 4 -> 2 px. A long "Linked to: name (group / local)" string used to stretch the popup arbitrarily; the label now shows `→ name` with the full origin in its tooltip, matching the short-label/tooltip rule. Verified by an offscreen `QWidget.grab()` render. No behaviour change — every widget attribute the handlers and the existing tests use is unchanged (`test_parameter_prior_widget.py` + `test_parameter_table_actions.py`: 24 passed; the one failure, `test_popup_edit_repaints_the_row_without_dispatching`, is **pre-existing test-order pollution** — it passes alone and fails identically with this change stashed).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: MATLAB
findings.source: * **FCS model catalogue expansion (PAM port, A/B-verified) + FLCS filter fixes.** Ported PAM's (Schrimpf 2018) FCS fit-model catalogue into `chisurf/core/models/fcs/models.yaml` as 13 absolute-`D`, physically-parametrised models (x in s; D µm²/s; w µm; tau µs): `FCS_D`, `FCS_D_2Component`, `FCS_D_2exp`, `FCS_TauD`, `FCS_TauD_anomalous`, `FCS_flow`, `FCS_D_Background`, `FCS_D_afterpulsing`, `FCS_TauD_Bleaching`, `FCS_2Focus_D` (two-focus absolute `D`), `FCS_FRETFCCS` (2-state kinetics), `nsFCS_ab_cd_triplet`, `FCS_Scanning`. Each carries the γ=1/√8 prefactor and triplet term. **A/B-verified**: `test/fitting/test_fcs_pam_ab.py` transcribes each PAM MATLAB `fit` lambda verbatim (keeping the `1e-12`/`1e-6` SI factors, which cancel in the diffusion terms → reduced `4·D·x/w²`) and asserts equality to the ChiSurf equation over random parameters (evaluated through the real `ParseModel` scanner). This replaced the initial hand-rolled `w0/s` two-focus entries. A catalogue-wide parse test also caught and fixed **3 pre-existing broken entries** (`3D Gauss, 1 exp. bunch, 1 stretched exp. bunch` — unbalanced parens + missing `a1`/`td1`; `Autocorrelation with biexponential anisotropy term` — `td`→`td1`; `1x2D Gauss, 1x3D Gauss, 1 bunching + 5 anti-correlation` — missing `s`), whose equations referenced parameters absent from their `initial:` blocks. **FLCS filters** (`chisurf/core/fluorescence/fcs/filtered.py`, PAM `Calc_fFCS_Filters` as reference): the weighted-pseudo-inverse algebra was already correct; added `rcond`/`tikhonov` conditioning + `filter_condition_number` diagnostic (for near-collinear/similar-lifetime patterns), `uniform_pattern` (flat afterpulsing/dark-count species → afterpulse-free FLCS), and `photon_filter_weights` (per-photon micro-time→filter weight, the core for wiring filters into a weighted correlator); fixed the legacy `calc_lifetime_filter` divide-by-zero (zero-bin guard) and removed its nonstandard global renormalisation that broke the `Σ_t R_k(t)·p_j(t)=δ_kj` relation. Tests: `test/fitting/test_fcs_pam_ab.py`, `test_fcs_2ffcs.py`, `test_fcs_filters.py` — 31 pass (arm64 env). Remaining gaps (correlator wiring of filters, channel-aware par/perp weighting, scatter/IRF & model-generated pattern species, non-Gaussian Dertinger MDF, and the pCF/SCCF/MIA models) documented in the new OKF concept [references/fcs-pam-port.md](/references/fcs-pam-port.md); [references/two-focus-fcs.md](/references/two-focus-fcs.md) and [plugins/fcs.md](/plugins/fcs.md) updated. PAM cloned under `junk/PAM` as reference.

findings.message: use a software role instead of: MATLAB
findings.source: * **New plugin `burst_ebfret` — binned-trajectory smFRET HMM (ebFRET port).** Closes the one confocal/TIRF gap the burst group lacked: analysis of **binned intensity-vs-time FRET traces** (wide-field/camera data) rather than photon streams. Added `chisurf/plugins/burst/burst_ebfret/` — a Qt-free, NumPy/SciPy-only port of ebFRET (van de Meent et al.; a re-implementation of vbFRET): `core/vbem.py` (per-trace variational-Bayes EM over a univariate Gaussian-emission HMM — Dirichlet priors on initial/transition, Normal-Gamma emission prior in ebFRET's `(m,β,a,b)` form, linear-scaled forward-backward), `core/ebayes.py` (empirical-Bayes outer loop with conjugate h-step prior updates ported from ebFRET's `+dist/{dirichlet,normgamma}/h_step.m` — Dirichlet Newton + Normal-Gamma moment-matching), `core/viterbi.py`, `core/analysis.py` (K-scan + evidence selection + dwell/transition decoding), `io.py` (ebFRET stacked `.dat` loader), `api/models.py`, `backend/services.py` (`burst_ebfret.jobs.compute` RPC), `cli/main.py` (`ebfret compute`). **Validated against ebFRET's own `simulated-K04-N350` fixture** (vendored under `tests/data/`, 350 traces / 39,595 frames): at K=4 the port recovers `[0.03, 0.34, 0.51, 0.62]`, the two well-separated interior states within 0.05 of ebFRET's fitted `[0.33, 0.516]` — endpoints differ only because this port fits the uncorrected proximity ratio `A/(D+A)` whereas ebFRET fits a background-subtracted signal (donor-only near 0). Tests: 7 fast synthetic unit tests + 4 recovery/integration tests (3 `slow`) all pass (arm64 env; pixi env solve is currently broken on an unrelated `msgpack` candidate). Porting this one algorithm covers the functionality of four MATLAB-only TIRF tools on fret.community (**ebFRET, vbFRET, HaMMy, SMACKS**). Scope: single-prior D=1 path; prior-mixture subpopulations, SMD/session I/O, and a GUI tool are follow-ups. Marked `experimental`/`menu_hidden`. Grew out of a fret.community/software gap analysis vs ChiSurf (repos cloned into `junk/`). Other gaps assessed (not built): diffusion-FRET photon simulation is already substantially in **tttrlib** (`~/dev/tttrlib`, PRD-005 Burbulator port — 3D Brownian + PSF + FRET + TCSPC + CLSM, SPC-132 byte-exact; remaining: periodic/mirror BCs, Photon-HDF5 write, single-molecule throughput) and needs only surfacing via chisurf **PRD-53**; rFRET ratiometric + FLIM crosstalk correction can reuse the existing forward crosstalk-matrix builder (`plugins/core/lightpath_simulator/backend/simulator.py::get_crosstalk_matrices`), which is currently never inverted to correct measured data; wide-field camera-movie TIRF (spot localization/trace extraction) remains a genuine large gap but is pure-intensity and off ChiSurf's photon-centric path (only PAM's TIFF-stack phasor-FLIM ingest is FLIM-relevant). See [plugins/burst.md](/plugins/burst.md).

findings.message: use a software role instead of: origin
findings.source: * **ChiMOL `cmd` gained PyMOL's core viewing/transform commands.** Added `turn`, `move`, `clip`, `rotate` and `translate` (RenderingMixin), the most-used PyMOL commands that were missing and that complement the new trackball navigation. Camera commands go cmd → `MolView` → `qtgl` renderer, all built on the rotation-matrix camera: `turn <x|y|z>, <angle>` left-multiplies the view rotation about a screen axis (Rodrigues); `move <x|y|z>, <dist>` pans (x/y) or dollies (z); `clip <near|far|slab|move>, <dist>` shifts the clip planes. `rotate <x|y|z>, <angle> [, sel]` and `translate [x,y,z] [, sel]` build a rigid transform and call `apply_transform_to_object` — verified `rotate x, 90` gives PyMOL's +90° ((0,1,0)→(0,0,1)) on the real `arr @ R^T` convention; fixed `MockViewer.apply_transform_to_object` (was `arr @ R`, missing the transpose) to match and gave it `turn`/`move`/`clip` stubs so the commands are testable headless. New `test_cmd_viewing.py` (**4**): registration, rotate/translate math, and camera-command dispatch. Chimol suite **89 passed**; lint net down (`cmd/rendering.py` 34→0 via cleanup, `qtgl`/`view` unchanged). More of PyMOL's surface (`create`, `set_name`, `dss`, `origin`, `count_atoms`, `save`, `run`) remains for follow-up. See [plugins/profiles/chimol.md](/plugins/profiles/chimol.md).
